extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the nature, aims, defects, and craft of poetry—how poetry should be conceived, what counts as good poetry, and common failings to avoid. Includes kinds of poetry, the poet's purpose, diction, meter, and moral/didactic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry defined (§1, §16 etc.): Poetry is distinguished from history and other arts by what it does — it treats what might be (general truth) rather than what has been; its essence lies in thought rather than merely in the 'apparelling of verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems primarily on their imaginative thought and the general truths they convey rather than only on their factuality or ornamental verse. The work of poetry is to propose what may be necessarily or probably true about characters and actions, not to chronicle particulars. Anti‑pattern: rewarding verse that is merely ornamental with little substantive imaginative or philosophical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's chief function: improving Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets improve Nature; they idealize man (not merely imitate). Poetry 'improves Nature' and 'idealize[s] man' rather than slavishly copying ordinary reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry refines and elevates natural experience—presenting idealized, instructive, or perfected versions of human character and action. Judge whether a poem enhances, clarifies, or perfects its subject rather than merely reproducing it. Example guidance in text: poets make general truths visible by shaping particulars into ideal examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral/political purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry best advances the end of all earthly learning, virtuous action. The poet's work furthers virtuous action and moral instruction in ways distinct from philosophers or historians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem contributes to moral imagination or virtuous behavior—does it inspire ethical reflection or exemplary conduct? Consider the poet's capacity to instruct indirectly by shaping desire and example. Anti‑pattern: poems that glamorize vice without critical framing or instructive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs. Philosophy and History (generality of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is more philosophical than history because it deals with universal or general truth (what kind of person would do or say a thing) rather than particular historical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by how well it captures character-types, typical motives, or universal situations. Prefer works that convey general human truths through imagined examples. Avoid conflating poetic success with historical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds and appropriate aims of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's kinds enumerated: (a) Divine, (b) Philosophical (perhaps too imitative), (c) Poetry proper, with further subdivisions of poetry proper (lyric, pastoral, epic, tragic, comic, heroic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing, identify the kind/subgenre and hold the work to the expectations of that kind (e.g., lyric's concision and musicality, epic's scope, pastoral's landscapes). Be cautious of mismatches between form and subject. The essay gives taxonomy and notes which kinds are fitting for which aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence in thought, not mere versification
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Its essence is in the thought, not in apparelling of verse.’ Poetry's core value is the intellectual and imaginative content, not ornamental language alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, strength, and originality of idea when evaluating poetry; metre, rhyme, and ornament should serve thought. Anti‑pattern: valuing clever surface devices when the underlying thought is tired or banal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Poet's Work and Parts (usefulness and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet's Work: what poetry does for us — creates pleasure, moves minds toward virtue and learning, and supplies 'what might be' to teach and delight. 'Poetry is the one creative art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem accomplishes the twin ends of delight and instruction: does it please the imagination while offering moral, intellectual, or emotional insight? Consider whether the poem's parts (plot, personae, diction, prosody) cohere to those ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hackneyed commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent resort to the Polyanthea and commonplace books caused many good quotations to become hackneyed; 'a common-place' came to mean a trite saying used without wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and composition should avoid overused quotations, clichés, and borrowed commonplaces that flatten original expression. Value freshness of image and argument over stock phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects in diction / antidote to Euphuism
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects in diction are identified (the essay attacks the artificial style 'Euphuism'). Poor diction—affected, overly ornamented, or unnatural language—counts against a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for naturalness, appropriateness, and clarity. Avoid the artificial, over‑polished 'Euphuistic' manner that trades sense for show. Prefer diction that fits the poet's purpose and the genre's demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects in specific genres (drama, lyric, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay lists defects specific to genres (e.g., defects in drama at an early stage of English theatre; defects in lyric poetry) and notes constraints of stage (no scenery) and stage practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge genre-specific works against the practical and aesthetic constraints of their form—e.g., drama should account for performance realities (stage limitations), lyric should maintain appropriate brevity and intensity, and epic/heroic forms should meet their scale and diction expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and Rhyme (prosodic competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and rhyme are singled out as important technical areas (section header 'Metre and Rhyme'). Prosody matters but is subordinate to thought and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical prosody — rhythm, metre, rhyme — for suitability and skill, ensuring it enhances rather than distracts from meaning. Anti‑pattern: strict technical virtuosity with no service to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice over mere knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Not knowledge but practice: the emphasis that poetic skill comes from doing rather than only from theoretical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value evidence of craft through practice (revision, performance, composition) when evaluating a poet's work; theoretical learning alone is insufficient. Look for living technique rather than only bookish theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to common objections to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief objections are rehearsed (poetry wastes time, is 'the mother of lies,' or 'the nurse of abuse,' and Plato's charge that poets should be banished). The essay meets these objections with counter‑arguments emphasizing poetry's usefulness and moral power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or evaluating poetry, be ready to address ethical and social objections: demonstrate how poetry instructs and reforms imagination rather than simply misleading. Evaluate whether a poem is ethically irresponsible or whether it renders vice critically and instructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and exemplarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry teaches by example — it presents typical characters and scenarios to show 'what kind of person would speak or act' in certain ways, making moral and psychological truth apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality and clarity of exemplars in a poem: are the characters and situations constructed to illuminate general truths or moral lessons? Prefer works that make instructive examples vivid and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to transcend disciplines (poet as synthesizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is described as 'monarch of all Human Sciences'—able to combine and surpass the work of philosophers, historians, and other learned persons through synthesis in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poets by their ability to integrate knowledge—philosophy, history, ethics—into imaginative form without merely paraphrasing didactic material. The best poetry combines learning with invention to create new insight.
